transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-10-29 14:00 PT
Duration: 52 mins
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Redwood CSM), Lena Torres (Valence Head of ML), Rajiv Kumar (Valence Platform), Sophie Lee (Valence PM), Tom Baxter (CTO)

Summary: quick weekly POC sync to review the latest cost/unit econ numbers, validate caching hit-rate improvements, and decide next experiments (24h A/B runs, latency deep dive). Slight transcription noise and a couple of overlapping talkers.

Topics: tokens/sec/$ trend, KV/prefix cache savings, batching config tradeoffs, routing policies, Dedicated vs hosted economics, next steps for validation.

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna run about 50 minutes, quick agenda, econ review, caching numbers, batching experiments and then next steps. Anyone got conflicts?
[00:22] Lena Torres: no, all good. excited to see the numbers, last week we saw a weird spike in p95 on Search rewrite route.
[00:35] Ethan Cole: yeah that was the one where batching got aggressive. we left the grouping window at 40ms to boost throughput and it pushed p95 up, i have the trade chart here in the sheet.
[00:48] Rajiv Kumar: i can confirm, around 10:40am PST we saw a sustained p95 bump to ~420ms. median looked okay.
[01:05] Sophie Lee: is that because of the model change we did to the 7b-quant variant? or because of request batching?
[01:18] Ethan Cole: mostly batching. the quantized model actually reduced token compute a bit, but the batching spike was causing queueing for some short requests. we measured tokens/sec/$ separately and the batched config improved tokens/sec/$ by ~2.1x for long-form routes.
[01:42] Tom Baxter: can you remind me how you're computing tokens/sec/$? Dave from infra asked when we did the VPC review.
[01:55] Ethan Cole: sure — our current metric is tokens per second per dollar of GPU spend normalized to the instance-hour cost. practical calc: total tokens served during the window divided by effective GPU-seconds consumed and then scaled to dollars using the committed hourly rate. i put the spreadsheet link in chat, but quick headline: hosted baseline for rwd-7b-q8 was about 1,800 tokens/sec/$ in the last run; with batching tuned for long requests that jumped to ~3,800 tokens/sec/$.
[02:28] Lena Torres: 1,800 to 3,800 sounds great, but are we seeing user-impacted latency for key routes? search is sensitive.
[02:40] Ethan Cole: yes, search (short prompts) saw p95 go from ~120ms to ~380ms when we were folding short and long together. we reverted the policy for the last 48h to separate low-latency and high-throughput buckets.
[02:58] Maya Patel: quick note — we also ran a prefix/KV cache experiment on the customer-support route. hit rate landed at 28% on sample, which translated to roughly 31% token cost savings for that route.
[03:15] Rajiv Kumar: 28% hit rate is pretty good; the tricky bit is cache priming for new docs. how are TTLs set?
[03:27] Ethan Cole: TTL is 6 hours for the pilot, we also have LRU eviction tuned to keep the working set small. priming helped — the warm-up job we recommended earlier boosted hit rate to the 28% baseline after the first 6 hours.
[03:42] Sophie Lee: did we measure user-visible latency when cache hits occur?
[03:47] Ethan Cole: cache hits reduced on-path latency by ~60ms median for support responses and of course avoided token generation. total cost effect is larger because some responses are entirely served from cached embeddings/mappings.
[04:03] Lena Torres: what about cold misses — any penalty on p95 when cache misses trigger model inference?
[04:10] Jordan Kim: i can add — we saw a small tail increase when misses coincide with batching windows, that's why splitting routes is helpful.
[04:19] Tom Baxter: i'm still wondering if Dedicated reserved capacity makes sense for the bulk of our traffic from a unit-econ perspective. can you compare quick numbers?
[04:32] Maya Patel: sure, short version: Dedicated committed nodes give you lower effective GPU-hour cost (we used a 12-month commit example in the sheet), so tokens/sec/$ improves maybe another 15-25% versus hosted for steady steady throughput. but you lose some flexibility and need to accept minimum commit sizes.
[04:51] Rajiv Kumar: any risk of underutilization? we have big diurnal swings.
[04:58] Ethan Cole: autoscale and burst policies help — you can keep a baseline commit for steady traffic and allow burst to hosted. fallback routing is automatic. we can model your traffic and show expected utilization curve.
[05:15] Sophie Lee: back to batching — is there an easy knob to prevent short requests from being grouped with long ones?
[05:23] Ethan Cole: yes, per-route latency thresholds + request grouping policies. we recommend a two-bucket approach: low-latency bucket with small window (5-10ms) and high-throughput bucket with larger window (40-60ms). default in your config now is already split but a previous change accidentally unified them for a subset of routes.
[05:45] Lena Torres: ok, next on caching: any best practices for shaping prompts to increase cacheability?
[05:53] Ethan Cole: consistent prompt templates help a lot — canonicalize system messages, remove variable timestamps/IDs from prompts that break prefix matches. we also suggest storing normalized keys for common intents so cache hits are higher.
[06:10] Tom Baxter: what's the impact of quantization — we tested q4 vs q8 last week, right?
[06:18] Ethan Cole: yes, q4_0 gave you roughly 18% compute reduction and a small drop in throughput latency in some ops, but output parity was pretty good for your use-cases. q8 was slightly faster in inference path on our stack due to kernel efficiency for that particular GPU, so the results were mixed — it's workload dependent.
[06:40] Rajiv Kumar: that matches our lab tests — q4 used less memory but introduced more fragmentation on multi-tenant instances, so throughput variability rose.
[06:51] Maya Patel: this is why we suggested running the 24h A/B: run q4 on the dedicated route and q8 on hosted for the same traffic slice and compare tokens/sec/$, p50/p95, and error rates.
[07:07] Sophie Lee: can you walk briefly through the tokens/sec/$ calc in the sheet? i opened the link.
[07:12] Ethan Cole: sure, column definitions: tokens served, GPU-seconds, effective hourly rate used, then tokens/(GPU-seconds) scaled with dollars. note we normalize to your contract hourly rate when showing Dedicated examples. for hosted we use the list-rate. there are a few assumptions pinned in the top of the sheet — e.g., avg prompt length, average generation length, retry rate.
[07:39] Lena Torres: since we have many short queries, the avg generation length assumption matters a lot. can we include a bucketed calc by route?
[07:47] Ethan Cole: yep we already added per-route tabs for Search, Support, and Paraphrase. i highlighted the Route-level tokens/sec/$ — Search produces lower tokens/sec/$ but has higher sensitivity to latency so you may accept a lower econ there.
[08:03] Tom Baxter: what about caching + batching synergy? do we double-count savings?
[08:09] Ethan Cole: good callout — we avoid double-counting by applying caching savings to reduced tokens served before batching gains. in practice the pipeline is: raw requests -> cache hits (drop tokens) -> remaining requests enter batching -> batching improves throughput. numbers in the sheet reflect that ordering.
[08:28] Rajiv Kumar: last week's anomalous spike, any root cause? we saw a retry storm from our clients after a 504 on our gateway.
[08:36] Maya Patel: yes we correlated the spike with higher retry rates causing queued work and pushing p95 up; when you reduced retries it came down. we recommended client-side jitter and exponential backoff.
[08:49] Sophie Lee: any security or compliance notes to consider if we enable cache aggressively? especially for support route that may contain PII.
[08:57] Ethan Cole: important point — Redwood's KV cache in the pilot is configured to honor PII flags from your preprocessing layer. by default we do not persist keys flagged as sensitive and TTLs are shorter. for enterprise Private deployments we can do customer-managed KMS and full audit logs.
[09:17] Lena Torres: just to confirm — are cached payloads encrypted at rest by default in hosted?
[09:22] Jordan Kim: yes, hosted uses encryption at rest; for additional control you can go Private with your own KMS.
[09:29] Tom Baxter: thinking about next actions for the team — we want a 24h A/B on Support route with cache on vs off, separate buckets for Search so latency doesn't regress, and a Dedicated modeling pass. does that capture it?
[09:42] Maya Patel: yes — Redwood to provide the updated batching JSON and modeling numbers (includes Dedicated commit example) by end of next week.
[09:50] Ethan Cole: i'll also export the raw tokens/sec/$ calc and include assumptions and per-route tabs.
[09:58] Rajiv Kumar: we'll enable trace sampling and share logs, and run the 24h A/B and send the telemetry.
[10:05] Sophie Lee: quick question about fallback policy — if Dedicated is saturated, will traffic go to hosted automatically?
[10:12] Maya Patel: yes, you can configure automated fallback to a compatible model in hosted region, and set priority rules by route. we can demo that flow in the next call.
[10:22] Lena Torres: curious — any simple heuristics to cap batching so we don't increase p95 above a target?
[10:28] Ethan Cole: yeah, the runtime supports per-route SLAs. you can set a target p95 in ms and the system will pick the batching window that maximizes tokens/sec/$ under that p95 constraint. it's not magic but it helps.
[10:44] Tom Baxter: do we have any rough estimate of cost savings if we adopt both caching and Dedicated commit for our top three routes?
[10:51] Maya Patel: ballpark from the model in the sheet: combined caching (30% effective token reduction on Support), batching tuned for high-throughput routes, plus a 12-month Dedicated commit could net you ~35-45% improvement in tokens/sec/$ across the portfolio versus current hosted baseline. exact depends on commit size and hit rates.
[11:12] Rajiv Kumar: good — if we can hit even the low end that's material. one operational ask: can we see per-token attribution for cost per route, not just aggregated?
[11:22] Jordan Kim: yes, Console shows per-route token counts and cost allocation; we can provide a sample export for accounting.
[11:30] Sophie Lee: any risks flagged for the pilot that we should be aware of?
[11:34] Ethan Cole: main risks: retry storms producing backlog, misconfigured batching windows causing latency regressions for short routes, and cold-cache misses during bursts. mitigations: client-side retry backoff, route split, cache priming jobs and shorter TTLs for sensitive data.
[11:52] Maya Patel: ok let's summarize next steps — Redwood share batching JSON + Dedicated modeling, Ethan share tokens/sec/$ export, Valence run 24h A/B + traces, and we'll set a latency deep-dive for 2026-11-09.
[12:05] Tom Baxter: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[12:10] Lena Torres: thanks all.
[12:15] End of recording

Notes: references in chat — "pilot-benchmarks-v2.xlsx" and "batching-config-v3.json" (links provided during call). A couple of speaker mislabels around 08:00 timestamp where two speakers overlapped.
